overview: A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically combine two branches because the same lines of a file were changed differently on each side, and Git needs a human to decide the final result.

Git merges by comparing both branches against their common ancestor (a three-way merge); when the two sides changed the same region, Git pauses, marks the file with conflict markers, and asks you to resolve it.

In data engineering, conflicts are routine on shared pipeline code, SQL models, DAG definitions, and requirements files; knowing how to read the markers, choose the right content, and finish the merge safely keeps the team unblocked without losing work.
learningObjectives: Explain why merge conflicts occur and how Git's three-way merge decides what is automatic versus manual.
Read and resolve conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) correctly, then stage and complete the merge or rebase.
Use tools like git status, git diff, git mergetool, git rerere, and abort/continue commands to resolve conflicts safely in real DE workflows.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A merge conflict is the state Git enters during a merge, rebase, cherry-pick, or stash-apply when it cannot reconcile divergent changes automatically. Git performs a three-way merge using the merge base (the common ancestor commit) and the two branch tips; when a hunk was modified on both sides relative to the base, Git writes both versions into the working-tree file surrounded by conflict markers and marks the path as unmerged in the index. The operation is suspended until the user edits the file to the desired final content, stages the resolution (git add), and completes the operation (git commit / git merge --continue / git rebase --continue) or aborts it.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Imagine two editors both revising the same paragraph of a shared document offline. When you try to combine their copies, changes to different paragraphs merge fine automatically, but where both edited the exact same sentence, the tool cannot know which wording you want. So it shows you both versions side by side with markers and says 'you decide.' A merge conflict is exactly that moment: Git hands you both versions of the clashing lines and waits for you to write the final version, save, mark it resolved, and finish.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Distributed version control (Git, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005) made branching cheap and parallel development the norm, which made merge conflicts an everyday event rather than a rare integration crisis. Git's three-way merge algorithm, inherited conceptually from earlier tools like diff3 and RCS, uses the common ancestor to distinguish additions from deletions. Git later added 'rerere' (reuse recorded resolution, 2006) to remember how repeated conflicts were resolved, and the 'zdiff3' conflict style (Git 2.35, 2022) to show the ancestor content inside markers, making resolutions less error-prone.

whyItMatters.business: Unresolved or badly resolved conflicts stall releases and can silently reintroduce bugs or drop features; a data team that resolves conflicts confidently ships pipeline changes faster and avoids costly data incidents caused by lost code.
whyItMatters.engineering: Conflict resolution is a core collaboration skill: it prevents overwriting a teammate's work, keeps history clean, and avoids the 'I just took my version' mistakes that erase changes and break shared modules, DAGs, and SQL models.
whyItMatters.scalability: As a team and codebase grow, more people touch the same files (config, requirements, orchestration DAGs); disciplined conflict resolution and small, frequent merges keep integration cost from exploding.
whyItMatters.cost: Time lost to tangled merges, reverting bad resolutions, and re-debugging dropped changes is expensive; resolving quickly and correctly the first time reduces engineering hours and incident cleanup.
whyItMatters.reliability: A wrong resolution can ship half-merged logic that passes review but corrupts data at runtime; careful, tested resolutions plus CI keep the merged result correct and deployable.

coreComponents.name: Three-way merge and the merge base
coreComponents.definition: Git compares each branch tip against their common ancestor (the merge base) to determine what each side changed, then combines non-overlapping changes automatically.
coreComponents.purpose: To merge as much as possible without human input and to precisely identify only the regions that truly conflict.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Find the common ancestor, compute per-file diffs for both sides, auto-apply non-overlapping hunks, and flag overlapping hunks as conflicts.
coreComponents.examples: git merge main | git merge-base HEAD feature/x | git log --merges

coreComponents.name: Conflict markers
coreComponents.definition: The <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> lines Git inserts into a file to delimit your current version, the incoming version, and (optionally) the common ancestor.
coreComponents.purpose: To show you exactly which lines clashed and from which side, so you can compose the correct final content.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Delimit the conflicting regions, label each side (HEAD/current vs incoming branch), and mark the file as unmerged until edited and staged.

coreComponents.name: Resolution and continuation commands
coreComponents.definition: The Git commands used to inspect, resolve, and finish a conflicted operation: git status, git diff, git add, git checkout --ours/--theirs, git merge/rebase --continue or --abort.
coreComponents.purpose: To edit the working tree to the desired result, mark it resolved, and either complete or safely cancel the merge/rebase.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Report unmerged paths, stage resolved files, allow taking one side wholesale, and resume or abort the in-progress operation.
coreComponents.examples: git status | git add app.py | git rebase --continue | git merge --abort

internalWorking: When you run git merge (or rebase/cherry-pick), Git locates the merge base commit and computes two diffs: base->ours and base->theirs. Hunks that changed on only one side are applied cleanly.

Where both sides changed overlapping lines relative to the base, Git cannot pick a winner, so it writes both versions into the working-tree file wrapped in conflict markers and records the path as 'unmerged' in the index with multiple stages (base, ours, theirs).

The merge/rebase operation is suspended: Git stores state (MERGE_HEAD or the rebase directory) so you can inspect, edit, and either continue or abort. Nothing is committed yet, so your history is untouched until you finish.

You edit each conflicted file to the final desired content, remove the markers, and run git add to collapse the unmerged stages into a single resolved blob in the index, signaling to Git that the conflict is settled.

Once all conflicts are staged, git commit (for merge) or git merge/rebase --continue records the result. If rerere is enabled, Git records the (pre-image -> resolution) mapping so an identical conflict is auto-resolved next time.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: git merge/rebase -> find merge base -> diff base vs ours & base vs theirs -> auto-apply non-overlapping hunks -> overlapping hunks written with conflict markers -> git status shows unmerged paths -> edit files to final content -> git add (mark resolved) -> git commit / --continue (or git merge --abort to cancel)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An engineer runs 'git pull' (or 'git merge main') on their feature branch to integrate the latest pipeline changes.
2. Git auto-merges most files but reports 'CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in dags/etl_orders.py' and leaves the working tree with markers.
3. The engineer runs 'git status' to list unmerged paths and 'git diff' to see the conflicting hunks with both sides labeled.
4. They open dags/etl_orders.py, combine the two versions into the correct final logic (keeping both the new retry policy and the new schedule), and delete all conflict markers.
5. They run 'git add dags/etl_orders.py' to stage the resolution, run the tests, then 'git commit' (merge) or 'git rebase --continue' to finish, producing a merged commit with a clean, correct file.

keyTerminology.meaning: The most recent commit both branches share; Git diffs each side against it to know what each branch actually changed.
keyTerminology.importance: Without the base, Git could not distinguish an added line from a deleted one; it is the foundation of accurate three-way merging.

keyTerminology.meaning: Text Git inserts to bracket the conflicting region: HEAD/ours above =======, incoming/theirs below, closed by >>>>>>>.
keyTerminology.importance: Reading them correctly is essential; leaving even one marker in the file breaks the code and often the build.

keyTerminology.meaning: 'Ours' is the branch you are on (HEAD during merge); 'theirs' is the branch being merged in. During a rebase these labels swap, which surprises many people.
keyTerminology.importance: Choosing --ours/--theirs blindly can discard needed work; understanding which side is which prevents accidental data loss.

keyTerminology.meaning: 'Reuse recorded resolution' - a Git feature that remembers how you resolved a specific conflict and replays it automatically next time the same conflict appears.
keyTerminology.importance: Saves large amounts of repeated effort during long-lived branches and repeated rebases.

importantConcepts.concept: Why conflicts are Git asking, not Git failing
importantConcepts.explanation: A conflict is not an error or corruption; it is Git explicitly refusing to guess. When two commits change the same lines relative to their shared ancestor, any automatic choice could silently destroy one person's intent, so Git stops and delegates the decision to a human who understands the code's meaning. Treating conflicts as a normal, expected part of collaboration - rather than a scary failure - leads to calmer, more correct resolutions. The right mindset is: 'Git preserved both intents and is asking me to reconcile them.'

importantConcepts.concept: Ours/theirs semantics differ between merge and rebase
importantConcepts.explanation: During 'git merge', HEAD is your branch, so 'ours' (--ours) is your work and 'theirs' is the branch you are merging in. During 'git rebase', Git replays your commits on top of the target, so from Git's perspective the target branch is temporarily checked out as HEAD - meaning 'ours' is the branch you are rebasing onto and 'theirs' is your own commit being reapplied. This inversion is a classic source of accidental data loss: engineers run 'git checkout --theirs' expecting their code and get the other side. Always confirm with git status/git diff before taking a whole side.

importantConcepts.concept: Resolve with meaning, not by picking a side
importantConcepts.explanation: Most real conflicts are not 'keep mine' or 'keep yours' - they require combining both intents. If a teammate added retry logic while you changed the schedule, the correct result usually contains both. Blindly taking one side (or accepting the first suggestion in an editor) is how features silently disappear. Read both versions, understand what each change was trying to do, and write the union that satisfies both, then run tests to confirm the merged logic actually works.

variationsAndTypes: **Content conflicts:** the same lines edited on both sides - the most common; resolved by editing the marked region.
**Add/add conflicts:** both branches created a new file with the same path but different content; Git marks the whole file conflicted.
**Modify/delete conflicts:** one side edited a file the other side deleted; you must decide to keep the edited file or accept the deletion.
**Rename conflicts:** a file renamed on one side and edited (or renamed differently) on the other; Git reports rename/rename or rename/modify conflicts.
**Conflict styles:** 'merge' (default, two sides) vs 'diff3'/'zdiff3' (also shows the common-ancestor version between markers), which makes intent much clearer.
**Where conflicts arise:** merge, rebase, cherry-pick, revert, and stash apply/pop can all produce the same conflict machinery.
advantages: **No silent data loss:** Git refuses to auto-pick, so nobody's work is discarded without a human decision.
**Precise scope:** three-way merging conflicts only the truly overlapping lines, auto-merging everything else.
**Recoverable:** an in-progress merge/rebase can always be aborted cleanly with --abort, returning to a safe state.
**Automatable repeats:** rerere and mergetools reduce the effort of recurring or large conflicts.
disadvantages: **Manual effort:** conflicts require human attention and understanding of the code, interrupting flow.
**Error-prone:** leaving a marker, taking the wrong side, or mis-combining logic can ship broken or incorrect code.
**Confusing semantics:** ours/theirs inversion during rebase and multi-file conflicts trip up even experienced engineers.
**Scales with divergence:** long-lived branches and infrequent integration produce large, painful conflicts.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Merge (creating a merge commit) is best for integrating shared/long-lived branches where preserving true history matters; rebase is best for keeping a feature branch's history linear and clean before it merges. Enable rerere and use diff3/zdiff3 style on any repo with frequent conflicts.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid rebasing branches others have already pulled (it rewrites shared history); avoid taking a whole side (--ours/--theirs) unless you are certain the other side's changes are unwanted; avoid letting branches diverge for weeks, which turns small conflicts into huge ones.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Two chefs are each given a copy of the same recipe card and told to improve it independently. One rewrites the sauce step; the other rewrites the plating step. When the head chef combines the cards, the different steps merge without issue - but where both rewrote the exact same 'add salt to taste' line differently, the head chef cannot guess which is intended. So they lay both versions of that one line on the counter (the conflict markers) and ask a person who understands the dish to write the final line, blending both ideas if needed, before the recipe goes to print (the commit).

commonMisconceptions.myth: A merge conflict means something is broken or Git made a mistake.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Conflicts are Git working correctly: it detected that both sides changed the same lines and safely declined to guess. It is a request for a decision, not an error, and no data is lost while it waits.

commonMisconceptions.myth: During resolution, 'ours' is always my code and 'theirs' is always the other branch.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That is true for merge, but rebase inverts it: 'ours' becomes the branch you are rebasing onto and 'theirs' your replayed commit. Always verify with git status/git diff before taking a whole side.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Keep branches short-lived and merge/rebase from main frequently so conflicts stay small; break large changes into smaller PRs so overlapping edits are rare and each conflict is trivial to resolve.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Never commit a resolution without removing every marker and running the test suite; a resolved-looking file with leftover markers or a wrong side selection ships broken logic that CI must catch.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Any conflicted merge/rebase can be aborted with git merge --abort / git rebase --abort to return to a known-good state; commit or stash your work before starting a risky merge so you always have a safe fallback.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Use CI to fail builds containing leftover conflict markers (grep for '<<<<<<<'), and require green checks plus review approval before a merged result lands on main.
productionConsiderations.security: Review merged changes to sensitive files (auth, credentials handling, CI configs) especially carefully, since a careless resolution can reintroduce a removed guard or leak a secret back into the tree.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Frequent small integrations cost minutes; deferred giant merges cost hours of untangling and re-testing - integrate early and often to minimize total effort.
productionConsiderations.performance: Enable git rerere and choose a clear conflict style (zdiff3) so repeated and complex conflicts resolve faster; use a visual mergetool for large or multi-file conflicts to reduce mistakes.

codeExamples.title: Producing and resolving a content conflict step by step
codeExamples.overview: A realistic flow: merge main into a feature branch, hit a conflict in a DAG file, inspect it, resolve by combining both changes, and complete the merge.
codeExamples.code:
# On your feature branch, integrate the latest main
$ git checkout feature/order-retries
$ git merge main
Auto-merging dags/etl_orders.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in dags/etl_orders.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

# See which files need attention
$ git status
On branch feature/order-retries
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")

Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
	both modified:   dags/etl_orders.py

# Inspect the conflicting hunk
$ git diff dags/etl_orders.py

# ...edit the file to combine both changes, remove all markers...

# Mark it resolved and finish the merge
$ git add dags/etl_orders.py
$ git commit --no-edit
[feature/order-retries 9f2c1ab] Merge branch 'main' into feature/order-retries
codeExamples.breakdown: git merge main triggers the three-way merge; the CONFLICT line names the file. git status lists it under 'Unmerged paths (both modified)'. After manually editing the file to the correct combined content and deleting the markers, git add collapses the unmerged stages and marks it resolved, and git commit records the merge commit. --no-edit accepts the default merge message.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in dags/etl_orders.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Committing while a marker (<<<<<<<) remains breaks the file at runtime. Running git add before actually resolving marks a still-conflicted file as done. Forgetting you are mid-merge and starting other work.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Run 'git config merge.conflictStyle zdiff3' so the diff shows the common ancestor, making it obvious what each side changed; enable 'git config --global rerere.enabled true' to auto-replay repeated resolutions.

codeExamples.title: Reading conflict markers and taking a whole side safely
codeExamples.overview: How to read the three-part marker block, and how to deliberately keep one side with git checkout --ours/--theirs when appropriate.
codeExamples.code:
# A conflicted region inside dags/etl_orders.py looks like this:
<<<<<<< HEAD
schedule_interval = "@hourly"   # your change
=======
retries = 3                      # incoming change from main
>>>>>>> main

# Correct resolution: keep BOTH intents, delete the markers ->
#   schedule_interval = "@hourly"
#   retries = 3

# When one whole side is genuinely correct (e.g. a regenerated lockfile):
$ git checkout --theirs poetry.lock   # take main's version entirely
$ git add poetry.lock

# To take YOUR branch's version of a file instead:
$ git checkout --ours config/prod.yaml
$ git add config/prod.yaml

# Changed your mind mid-merge? Return to a clean pre-merge state:
$ git merge --abort
codeExamples.breakdown: Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your (ours) version; between ======= and >>>>>>> main is the incoming (theirs) version. Most resolutions keep both by editing to the union and deleting markers. git checkout --ours/--theirs takes an entire file from one side and is only safe when you are sure the other side's edits are unwanted. git merge --abort cancels everything and restores the pre-merge state.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Mixing up --ours and --theirs (they invert during rebase) discards needed work. Using --theirs on a file that also had valuable local edits silently loses them. Forgetting to git add after checkout leaves the file still unmerged.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Before taking a side, run 'git diff --ours <file>' and 'git diff --theirs <file>' to confirm exactly what each contains; for many recurring conflicts, prefer editing to the true union over blanket --ours/--theirs.

codeExamples.title: Using a visual mergetool and finishing a rebase conflict
codeExamples.overview: Launch a GUI mergetool for complex conflicts, then resolve and continue a rebase (where ours/theirs are inverted).
codeExamples.code:
# Configure and launch a visual three-way merge tool (e.g. VS Code)
$ git config --global merge.tool vscode
$ git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait $MERGED'
$ git mergetool
Merging:
dags/etl_orders.py
Normal merge conflict for 'dags/etl_orders.py':
  {local}: modified file
  {remote}: modified file

# During a REBASE the labels invert: 'ours' = branch you rebase ONTO
$ git rebase main
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in dags/etl_orders.py
$ git status
interactive rebase in progress; onto a1b2c3d
# ...resolve the file, then...
$ git add dags/etl_orders.py
$ git rebase --continue
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/order-retries.
codeExamples.breakdown: git mergetool opens each conflicted file in a configured GUI showing local/remote/base panes so you can pick lines visually, then it stages the result. During a rebase, Git replays your commits onto main, so 'ours' is main and 'theirs' is your commit - the inverse of merge. After editing and git add, git rebase --continue reapplies the remaining commits.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming ours/theirs behave like merge during a rebase, then taking the wrong side. Mergetool leaving .orig backup files (disable with mergetool.keepBackup false). Abandoning a rebase halfway without --abort, leaving a detached, confusing state.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Set 'git config --global mergetool.keepBackup false' to avoid .orig clutter; enable rerere so a long rebase with the same recurring conflict resolves the repeated hunks automatically.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: Two data engineers work in parallel on the orders ETL: one adds a retry policy to the DAG, the other changes its schedule and updates requirements.txt. When both open pull requests against main, the second to merge hits conflicts and must integrate cleanly without dropping the first engineer's retry logic or shipping broken code.
endToEndExample.inputData: A Git repository with branch main plus two feature branches touching the same files: dags/etl_orders.py (both modified the DAG config) and requirements.txt (both bumped different package pins).
endToEndExample.architecture: Feature branches -> pull request -> CI (lint, tests, marker check) -> merge into main. Conflict resolution happens locally on the second branch by merging (or rebasing) main in, resolving markers, and re-running tests before pushing.
processingSteps: 1. First engineer's PR merges to main cleanly, adding retries=3 to the DAG and bumping pandas in requirements.txt.
2. Second engineer runs 'git checkout feature/schedule && git merge main' and gets CONFLICT in both dags/etl_orders.py and requirements.txt.
3. They run git status and git diff to see both sides; in the DAG they keep BOTH retries=3 (from main) and their new schedule_interval, deleting all markers.
4. In requirements.txt they keep both dependency bumps (pandas from main, requests from their branch), producing a superset with no markers.
5. They git add both files, run the test suite and a 'grep -R "<<<<<<<"' marker check, then git commit and push; CI passes and the PR merges.
endToEndExample.output: A merged main branch whose dags/etl_orders.py contains both the retry policy and the new schedule, and whose requirements.txt contains both dependency bumps, with no conflict markers and all tests green.
endToEndExample.monitoring: CI runs a grep for leftover conflict markers and fails the build if any exist; test and lint jobs verify the merged logic; branch-protection requires green checks and a review before merge.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: If the resolution looks wrong mid-merge, the engineer runs git merge --abort to return to a clean state and retries; if a wrong side was taken, they re-open the file, restore the missing lines from git log/git show, and re-resolve.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Both engineers' changes ship intact on main, history clearly records the merge, and the pipeline runs with both the new schedule and retry behavior - no work lost, no broken markers deployed.

industryUseCases.company: Analytics teams using dbt / SQL models in Git
industryUseCases.problem: Many analysts edit the same shared SQL models and schema YAML files, producing frequent content conflicts on model logic and column definitions.
industryUseCases.solution: Short-lived branches, frequent rebase from main, zdiff3 conflict style, and careful union resolutions that keep both analysts' column changes; CI checks for leftover markers and runs dbt tests.
industryUseCases.benefits: Fast, correct integration of parallel analytics work with no silently dropped columns and a clean, reviewable history.

industryUseCases.company: Platform teams managing Airflow DAG repositories
industryUseCases.problem: DAG definitions and shared operators are edited concurrently, so schedule, retry, and dependency changes collide when branches merge.
industryUseCases.solution: Enable rerere for recurring conflicts on generated files, use a visual mergetool for complex DAG conflicts, and require tests plus a marker-check job before merge.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reliable DAG deployments where concurrent changes are combined correctly and repeated conflicts resolve automatically.

industryUseCases.company: ML/data platform teams with lockfiles (poetry.lock, requirements.txt)
industryUseCases.problem: Dependency lockfiles conflict constantly because every branch regenerates them, creating large, noisy conflicts.
industryUseCases.solution: Resolve by regenerating the lockfile after merging (take one side then re-lock), or configure a merge driver for the lockfile; enforce a single source of truth for pins.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consistent, buildable dependency sets across branches without hand-editing thousands of conflicted lockfile lines.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Conflict cost grows with branch divergence and file contention, so scale collaboration by keeping PRs small and short-lived, integrating main frequently, and splitting hot files (giant config or DAG files) into smaller modules that different people can edit without overlapping.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Every conflicted operation is reversible: git merge/rebase/cherry-pick --abort restores the pre-operation state, and because nothing is committed until you finish, the shared history is never left in a broken state by an in-progress resolution.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Branch protection ensures main is always deployable: merges require green CI (including a leftover-marker check) and review, so a bad resolution cannot reach the deployable branch even if a conflict was resolved carelessly locally.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Git's reflog (git reflog) records where branches pointed before a merge/rebase, so a botched resolution can be undone by resetting to the pre-merge commit; keeping the original branch until the PR merges provides an additional safety copy.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Enable rerere to auto-replay repeated resolutions during long rebases, use zdiff3 style to speed up manual resolution, and adopt merge drivers for machine-generated files (lockfiles) so humans never hand-resolve them.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Frequent small integrations turn multi-hour merge marathons into minutes; investing minutes to rebase daily is far cheaper than the hours spent untangling a branch that diverged for weeks.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Treat resolutions to security-sensitive files (auth, secret handling, CI/CD, .github workflows) as high-risk: a careless merge can silently reintroduce a removed check or restore a leaked credential, so require focused review of those diffs.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: CI jobs that grep for conflict markers, run tests, and diff the merged result against expectations make bad resolutions visible before deploy; PR templates prompt authors to confirm they combined both intents.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: For pipeline code, run data tests (schema checks, row counts, dbt tests) on the merged branch so a wrong resolution that changes transformation logic is caught before it corrupts production data.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Descriptive merge commit messages and PR discussions log how a nontrivial conflict was resolved; CI alerts on marker-check or test failures so a broken resolution never merges silently.

recommendedPractices: **Integrate early and often:** merge or rebase main into your branch daily so conflicts stay small and easy to reason about.
**Resolve by combining intents:** read both sides, understand each change, and write the union - do not blindly pick a side.
**Always remove every marker and run tests** before staging and committing a resolution.
**Use git status and git diff first** to see the full scope before editing anything.
engineeringStandards: Enable a clear conflict style (git config merge.conflictStyle zdiff3) repo-wide so the common ancestor is visible.
Enable rerere (rerere.enabled true) to auto-replay repeated resolutions during long rebases.
Add a CI check that fails the build if any conflict marker string remains in the tree.
designRecommendations: Split large, high-contention files (monolithic config, giant DAG files) into smaller modules to reduce overlapping edits.
Use merge drivers or a regenerate-then-relock policy for machine-generated files like lockfiles instead of hand-editing them.
Prefer rebase for a clean linear feature history and merge commits for integrating shared long-lived branches.
namingConventions: Name branches by intent and owner (feature/order-retries, fix/schema-drift) so conflicting work is easy to trace.
Write merge commit messages that state what was combined when a conflict was nontrivial.
Tag or note the pre-merge commit if you might need to roll a resolution back.
documentationStandards: Document the team's chosen integration strategy (merge vs rebase) and conflict-style settings in the repo README/CONTRIBUTING.
Note in PRs how significant conflicts were resolved, especially for security- or data-critical files.
Document merge-driver configuration for generated files so the whole team benefits.
testingStrategies: Run the full test suite on the merged result, not just on each branch in isolation.
Add a grep-based check for leftover conflict markers to CI and to a local pre-commit hook.
For data pipelines, run data/schema tests on the merged branch to catch resolutions that alter transformation logic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing a file that still contains conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The engineer resolves most hunks, misses one, and git add + commit without re-scanning the file or running tests.
commonMistakes.impact: The code is syntactically broken and fails at runtime or breaks the build; if it slips past CI it can crash a pipeline in production.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Search every resolved file for marker strings (grep -R '<<<<<<<') and run tests before staging; add a CI/pre-commit check that blocks markers.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blindly taking one whole side with git checkout --ours/--theirs (especially during a rebase where they invert).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels like a quick fix, and people assume ours=my code always; rebase silently swaps the meaning.
commonMistakes.impact: The other side's legitimate changes are discarded, silently deleting a teammate's feature or your own commit's work.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Verify with git diff --ours/--theirs first, prefer editing to the true union, and only take a whole side when you are certain the other is unwanted.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting a feature branch diverge from main for weeks before integrating.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Focusing on the feature and avoiding merges that feel disruptive; underestimating how fast main moves.
commonMistakes.impact: A massive, tangled conflict across many files that is slow and error-prone to resolve, risking dropped changes.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Rebase or merge main into the branch frequently (daily) so each conflict is tiny and easy to resolve correctly.

comparisonSection.explanation: Merge preserves true history and is safe for shared/long-lived branches, but creates merge commits and (with default style) can make history noisier. Rebase produces a clean linear history ideal for feature branches before merging, but rewrites commits (so never rebase branches others already pulled) and inverts ours/theirs during conflicts. Choose merge for integrating shared branches and rebase for tidying a private feature branch.

The default merge style shows only ours and theirs, so you cannot always tell what the original was or which side actually changed a line. diff3/zdiff3 inserts the merge-base version between the markers, making each side's intent explicit and greatly reducing wrong resolutions. zdiff3 additionally trims common lines for a tighter view. diff3/zdiff3 is recommended for any repo with frequent conflicts.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a merge conflict and why does it happen?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A merge conflict occurs when Git tries to combine two branches and both changed the same lines of a file differently relative to their common ancestor. Git can auto-merge non-overlapping changes but refuses to guess which overlapping change wins, so it marks the file and asks a human to resolve it.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress that a conflict is Git being safe, not failing - it preserves both intents and requests a decision. Mention the three-way merge and common ancestor.

beginnerQuestions.question: What do the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers mean?
beginnerQuestions.answer: They delimit a conflict: content between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your current branch's version (ours); content between ======= and >>>>>>> branchname is the incoming version (theirs). You edit the region to the final content and delete all three markers before staging.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Note that leaving any marker breaks the file, and with diff3/zdiff3 style a third section shows the common ancestor.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you resolve a conflict without losing either side's work?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Run git status to find unmerged files and git diff to see both sides. Open each file, understand what each side intended, and edit the marked region into the union that satisfies both changes, removing all markers. Then git add each file and finish with git commit (merge) or git rebase --continue, after running tests.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize combining intents over picking a side, and re-running tests. Mention grep for markers as a safety check.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between --ours and --theirs, and why is it tricky during a rebase?
intermediateQuestions.answer: --ours takes the current branch's (HEAD's) version of a file and --theirs takes the incoming branch's version. During a merge, ours is your branch. During a rebase, Git checks out the target branch as HEAD and replays your commits, so ours becomes the branch you're rebasing onto and theirs becomes your own commit - the meanings invert, which commonly causes accidental data loss.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key insight is the inversion during rebase; always verify with git diff before taking a whole side.

advancedQuestions.question: What is git rerere and when would you use it?
advancedQuestions.answer: rerere ('reuse recorded resolution') records the mapping from a conflict's pre-image to how you resolved it, then automatically replays that resolution the next time the identical conflict appears. It's invaluable during long-lived branches and repeated rebases where the same conflict recurs, saving you from re-resolving it each time. Enable it with git config --global rerere.enabled true.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show you understand it stores resolutions per-conflict-signature and only auto-applies to identical conflicts, not arbitrary ones.

advancedQuestions.question: How do you handle conflicts in machine-generated files like lockfiles?
advancedQuestions.answer: Don't hand-edit them. Take one side (usually main's), then regenerate the lockfile from the merged manifest (e.g., re-run pip-compile/poetry lock), or configure a custom merge driver in .gitattributes so Git regenerates instead of textually merging. This avoids massive, error-prone manual resolutions and guarantees a consistent, resolvable lockfile.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates knowing that some files should be regenerated, not merged, and that .gitattributes merge drivers exist.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You rebased your feature branch onto main, ran git checkout --theirs on a conflicted file expecting to keep your code, and now your changes are gone. What happened and how do you recover?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: During rebase, ours/theirs invert: 'theirs' is actually your replayed commit and 'ours' is main - but the engineer's expectation is backwards, so they likely took the wrong side or misread. First determine the correct final content, then recover the lost lines from history. The rebase can be aborted or the file restored from the original commit.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Recognize the ours/theirs inversion under rebase. If still mid-rebase, run git rebase --abort to return to the pre-rebase branch and start over, this time verifying with git diff --ours/--theirs before choosing. If already finished, use git reflog to find the pre-rebase commit or git show <original-commit>:<file> to recover the lost lines, then re-resolve keeping both sides.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a branching and conflict-management workflow for a 20-person data team sharing one repo of DAGs, SQL models, and requirements files.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Adopt short-lived feature branches off main with mandatory PRs and branch protection. Standardize settings via repo config (.gitattributes, conflictStyle=zdiff3, rerere enabled). Add CI jobs for lint, tests, data tests, and a leftover-marker check. Use merge drivers/regeneration for lockfiles and split high-contention files into modules.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Rebase gives clean history but rewrites commits (risky if shared); merge preserves history but adds merge commits. Strict CI and small PRs add process overhead but drastically cut integration pain and prevent bad resolutions from reaching main.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Encourage daily integration from main, keep PRs small, modularize hot files so fewer people edit the same lines, and rely on rerere plus merge drivers so recurring/machine-generated conflicts resolve automatically as the team and codebase grow.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: A merge conflict is Git pausing a merge/rebase/cherry-pick because both sides changed the same lines relative to their common ancestor, marking the file so you can edit it to the correct final content, stage it, and finish.
keyConcepts: Conflicts are Git safely asking for a decision, not an error - no work is lost while it waits.
Markers: <<<<<<< HEAD (ours) / ======= / >>>>>>> branch (theirs); zdiff3 also shows the ancestor.
ours/theirs invert between merge and rebase - always verify with git diff before taking a whole side.
Resolve by combining both intents, remove every marker, then git add and continue/commit.
Any conflicted operation is reversible with --abort; reflog recovers from a bad finished resolution.
commands: git merge main   # start a merge; conflicts pause it
git status   # list unmerged (both modified) paths
git diff [--ours|--theirs] <file>   # inspect the conflict / each side
git add <file>   # mark a resolved file
git commit --no-edit   # finish a merge after resolving
git rebase --continue   # finish a rebase after resolving
git checkout --ours|--theirs <file>   # take one whole side
git merge --abort   /   git rebase --abort   # cancel and restore
git config merge.conflictStyle zdiff3   # show common ancestor
git config --global rerere.enabled true   # replay repeated resolutions
git reflog   # recover the pre-merge/rebase commit
interviewPoints: Three-way merge uses the common ancestor to decide auto vs manual.
Marker anatomy: ours above =======, theirs below, closed by >>>>>>>.
ours/theirs inversion during rebase is a classic data-loss trap.
Resolve by union of intents, then remove markers and test.
rerere, zdiff3, and merge drivers make conflicts cheaper and safer.
quickNotes: Grep for '<<<<<<<' before committing to catch leftover markers.
Set mergetool.keepBackup false to avoid .orig files.
Regenerate lockfiles instead of hand-merging them.
Integrate main daily to keep conflicts small.
git merge --abort is always a safe escape hatch.

keyTakeaways: A merge conflict is Git working correctly: it detected that both branches changed the same lines relative to their common ancestor and safely declined to guess, preserving both intents and asking you to write the final version.

Read the markers precisely - ours above =======, theirs below - and remember that ours/theirs invert during a rebase, a classic cause of accidental data loss; always verify with git diff before taking a whole side.
Resolve by combining both sides' intent rather than blindly picking one, delete every marker, run the tests, then git add and finish with commit or --continue.
Any conflicted merge/rebase/cherry-pick is fully reversible with --abort, and git reflog can recover the pre-operation state after a bad resolution, so conflicts are never a point of no return.

Keep conflicts small and cheap by integrating main frequently, splitting high-contention files, enabling zdiff3 and rerere, and adding a CI check that blocks leftover conflict markers from ever reaching main.
